Subject: Dedicated sizing request — 32k context model + quantization question

Hi Karthik,

Thanks again for the call this morning. To summarize our ask: AsterBio is moving a critical product path onto a dedicated pool and we need a capacity recommendation tied to expected SLAs. Key details:
- Model: open-architecture 32k context generative model (we will provide final weights during onboarding).
- Typical workload: 25–40 RPS peak (bursty during analysis windows), median request length 4k tokens, tail up to 20k generation tokens in some workflows.
- Session reuse: heavy prefix reuse across batches (approx 60% overlap); we rely heavily on KV cache to avoid re-encoding long contexts.
- Desired optimizations: quantized inference (we are open to q4_0 / int8 strategies) to reduce GPU TCO, but latency must stay sub-350ms p50 for short-chat flows and p95 < 1.2s for long runs where possible.

Questions for Redwood team:
1) Rough GPU pool sizing (N GPUs) for a reserved capacity commitment to cover 40 RPS steady with 4k median, and separate estimate for 25–40 RPS burst profile with the 20k tail.
2) How much memory headroom do we need for KV cache at 32k context (per session) under different quantization choices?
3) Any operational suggestions (prefix caching, sticky session routing, or special tiling) to reduce reserved footprint while preserving latency SLOs?

I've attached a short CSV of our measured per-request token distribution and a short note from our infra team. Happy to jump on a technical deep-dive if helpful.

Thanks,
Elena
Head of Platform
AsterBio

Clarifying items for accuracy:
- Can you confirm the fraction of requests that are read-only (embedding/query) vs. generation? Our sizing differentiates memory/throughput for each.
- Do you plan to pin a single model variant or expect a mix (e.g., small/fast fallback + full 32k)?
- Any hard SLA on p99? (p95 targets you listed give a good starting point; we often recommend a higher-availability fallback path).

What I'll do next: I'll run a quick KV-window memory simulation and have initial GPU-counts for three quantization scenarios (fp16 baseline, q4/admix, and int8 where applicable). Priyom — can you run the short sim with the attached token distribution and produce a per-session KV size + ephemeral workspace for the 3 quant modes? Karthik / Marissa — ran the quick sim and scribbled the key numbers. Attaching a compact PDF with the sim traces; pasted the highlights below. Note: these are conservative (assume model weights loaded once per GPU, typical runtime memory overheads included).

Simulation assumptions (short):
- Model weights footprint: 40 GB FP16 baseline (will be ~10–12 GB after q4_0-style quantization metadata + 6–8 GB for int8 variant depending on kernel support).
- KV cache (per active session, full 32k context): ~1.9 GB/session (FP16 tokens) before quantization of KV. With q4-style storage we estimate ~0.9 GB/session; int8 can reach ~0.6 GB/session but requires runtime support and may increase compute cost per token.
- Workspace & ephemeral buffers per request: 1.0–1.5 GB depending on sequence length and attention implementation.

Sizing outputs (rounded):
1) Baseline FP16 (no quant):
- 40 RPS steady (median 4k tokens, 60% prefix reuse): ~16 GPUs (A100-class equivalent), reserved pool. This assumes 6 concurrent sessions per GPU for long-run occupancy and conservative batching for latency SLOs.
- Peak 40 RPS with 20k tails: add 6–8 GPUs for headroom (total ~22–24).

2) Q4-style (q4_0 / blockwise 4-bit KV storage):
- Per-session KV reduced ~2x; model weights down to ~12–14 GB.
- 40 RPS steady: ~10 GPUs. Peak with tails: ~14–16 GPUs.

3) Int8 aggressive mode (where kernels available):
- Model weights ~6–8 GB; KV ~0.6 GB/session. But note: int8 compute can increase latency for generative workloads because of extra scaling casts or fallback kernels.
- 40 RPS steady: ~8 GPUs. Peak: ~11–13 GPUs.

Operational recommendations (short list):
- Heavy prefix reuse -> enable sticky routing with per-customer KV hot-cache affinity to avoid reloading KV across GPUs. That reduces live-session memory churn and improves p50 latency.
- Use two-tier pool: reserved pool sized to q4 estimates + small burst pool (preemptible or shared) for tail traffic; automated fallback from reserved->burst on queueing.
- For strict latency flows, prefer q4 for model + q4 KV storage and reserve a small int8-capable pool for cost-heavy batch jobs where latency is relaxed.
- KV eviction policy: TTL + LRU tuned to the 60% reuse figure, and a tiny persistent prefix-cache for the top 5% of sessions.

Quick throughput rule-of-thumb: for this model family, 1 GPU handles ~2.5–4 RPS of medium-length generative work depending on quantization/batching. Use conservative end of range for reserved commitments.

I'll attach the sim PDF and a CSV with per-session memory breakdown for the three modes.

-priyom
Solution Architect, Redwood Inference

Elena — concise answers and a recommended commitment for your deck below. Attached: one-pager with the recommended reserved pool and fallback policy.

Short answers:
- Latency regression q4 -> int8: we observe on this model family that single-token latency can increase ~5–15% in int8 on current runtimes if fallback kernels are used. For long-tail generation (20k tokens) throughput can improve in int8 (fewer memory-bound stalls), but end-to-end p95 may be worse if kernels fallback to slower paths. Recommendation: q4 for reserved low-latency flows; int8 for batch/analytics only.
- Sticky routing: handled best at the orchestrator layer with a lightweight affinity service (we provide reference Helm chart). It stores KV pointers locally and can use a Redis-like metadata store for session indices; the heavy KV stays on-GPU. We recommend using your existing Redis for metadata + the Redwood affinity controller.
- Procurement uplift: use a +20% uplift on top of the q4 recommended reserved pool to cover growth and a two-week burst window. That typically balances cost vs. overcommit risk.

Recommended 3-line summary per quant mode + reserved N (for deck):
- FP16 baseline: high-latency headroom, large weights (40 GB). Recommended reserved pool: 16 GPUs. Uplift: +20% -> ask for 19 GPUs. Use only if you need guaranteed no-quant accuracy parity.
- Q4-style (recommended for reserved): 2x KV reduction, moderate weight compression (12–14 GB). Recommended reserved pool: 10 GPUs. Uplift: +20% -> ask for 12 GPUs. Good balance of latency and cost; preserves p50/p95 for interactive flows.
- Int8 (cost-optimized, selective): smallest footprint but risk of kernel fallbacks; use for batch analytics or non-interactive long jobs. Recommended reserved pool (if you pick int8): 8 GPUs. Uplift: +20% -> ask for 10 GPUs.

Fallback model variant plan: reserve a smaller 8k-context fast variant (q4) pinned for sub-350ms interactive flows for cases where long-tail generation would push latency past thresholds. Automatic A/B-based routing can use the fast variant for 90% of UI interactions and escalate to full 32k model for deep analysis jobs.
